paragraphs.title: A Request to Be Heard and the Shock It Causes

easy.explanation: Job asks his friends to hear his speech.
easy.q: Whom does Job ask to hear his speech?

easy.explanation: Job says, “Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on.”
easy.q: What does Job ask his friends to do before they mock?

answers: Fear and trembling take hold of him
easy.explanation: Job says that when he remembers, he is afraid and trembling takes hold of his flesh.
easy.q: What happens to Job when he remembers his situation?

medium.explanation: He asks to speak first, after which they may mock or respond.
medium.q: Why does Job ask his friends to wait before responding?

answers: They may mock after he speaks
They must leave after he speaks
medium.explanation: Job permits them to mock him after he has finished speaking.
medium.q: What does Job mean by, “after that I have spoken, mock on”?

medium.explanation: Job asks, “As for me, is my complaint to man?” and directs his concern toward God.
medium.q: To whom is Job’s complaint ultimately directed?

answers: He does not wish to speak
challenge.explanation: The request emphasizes that his words deserve serious and astonished attention.
challenge.q: What does Job’s request to lay a hand upon the mouth show about his words?

answers: Remembering makes him forget his suffering
Remembering his situation causes fear and trembling
challenge.explanation: Job says that even when he remembers, fear and trembling seize him.
challenge.q: What connection does Job make between remembering and trembling?

answers: To request a hearing before presenting his complaint
challenge.explanation: The opening asks the friends to listen before Job presents his difficult argument.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of Job’s opening words?

short_answers.question: What does Job ask his friends to do before they mock him?
short_answers.answer: He asks them to suffer him to speak first.
short_answers.explanation: Job says, “Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on.”

paragraphs.title: The Prosperity and Peace of the Wicked

answers: They live, grow old, and become mighty
easy.explanation: Job asks why the wicked live, become old, and are mighty in power.
easy.q: What happens to the wicked according to Job?

easy.explanation: Their houses are safe from fear, and the rod of God is not upon them.
easy.q: What is the condition of the houses of the wicked?

easy.explanation: Their little ones are sent forth like a flock, and their children dance.
easy.q: What do the children of the wicked do?

answers: Peaceful houses, established offspring, and joy
medium.explanation: Job describes their secure homes, successful descendants, and joyful children.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the prosperity of the wicked?

medium.explanation: They say, “Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways.”
medium.q: What do the wicked say to God?

medium.explanation: They ask, “What is the Almighty, that we should serve him?”
medium.q: What do the wicked ask about serving the Almighty?

answers: The wicked are described as living, strong, and secure
challenge.explanation: Their lives appear prosperous and peaceful rather than visibly punished.
challenge.q: What difficulty does Job present to the idea that the wicked are punished immediately?

answers: They enjoy prosperity but reject God
They are poor but serve God
They have no children but rejoice
challenge.explanation: They enjoy security and prosperity while saying they do not desire God’s ways.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in Job’s description of the wicked?

answers: They question the benefit of serving God
They are thankful for their success
challenge.explanation: The wicked express contempt for the usefulness of prayer and service.
challenge.q: What does the statement, “what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?” reveal?

paragraphs.title: The Absence of Visible Retribution and God’s Ways

answers: How often it is put out
easy.explanation: Job asks, “How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!”
easy.q: What does Job ask about the candle of the wicked?

answers: Stubble and chaff carried by the wind
easy.explanation: They are compared to stubble before the wind and chaff carried by a storm.
easy.q: What are the wicked compared to when destruction comes?

easy.explanation: Job asks, “Shall any teach God knowledge?”
easy.q: Can a person teach God knowledge?

answers: He says God should reward the wicked person himself
medium.explanation: Job says that God may lay up iniquity for the children, but He rewards the wicked man himself.
medium.q: Why does Job reject the idea that punishment should simply fall on the children?

medium.explanation: Chaff is light material blown away by a storm, making it a picture of helplessness.
medium.q: What is chaff in the comparison of the wicked?

answers: Because their punishment is always obvious
Because their visible punishment is not consistent
Because only the righteous are punished
medium.explanation: Job questions why the wicked’s candle and destruction are not always visibly brought upon them.
medium.q: Why does Job ask about the candle and destruction of the wicked?

answers: He does not see a consistent visible connection between wickedness and punishment
He claims there is no death
He claims everyone understands God’s judgment
challenge.explanation: Job observes that the wicked are not always visibly punished during their lives.
challenge.q: What is the basic difficulty Job raises about the punishment of the wicked?

answers: They cannot compel God to give an account
challenge.explanation: Job emphasizes that no person can force God to explain or repay according to human demands.
challenge.q: What does “who shall repay him what he hath done?” suggest about human beings?

answers: The children should be punished instead
The wicked person himself should know the reward of his deeds
challenge.explanation: Job distinguishes the children from the punishment and responsibility of the wicked person.
challenge.q: How does Job’s discussion of the children relate to personal responsibility?

paragraphs.title: Two Different Lives and One Common Death

answers: Dying in full strength and peace
easy.explanation: He dies in his full strength, wholly at ease and quiet.
easy.q: How is the first person described?

answers: Dying in bitterness and without pleasure
easy.explanation: The second dies in the bitterness of his soul and never eats with pleasure.
easy.q: How is the second person described?

answers: They lie alike in the dust and are covered by worms
easy.explanation: Job says that both lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.
easy.q: What happens to both people after death?

answers: Peace and abundance versus bitterness and deprivation
medium.explanation: One dies peacefully and comfortably, while the other dies bitterly and without pleasure.
medium.q: What contrast does Job place between the two people?

answers: He dies while healthy and at ease
He dies after losing his home
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a person who dies in strength, peace, and comfort.
medium.q: What does “in his full strength” communicate about the first person?

answers: Their different earthly conditions do not remain in burial
medium.explanation: Despite their very different lives, both share the same final burial.
medium.q: What follows from the fact that both people lie down alike in the dust?

answers: People may have very different lives but share a similar death
Every wicked person is punished immediately
challenge.explanation: Job contrasts their lives while showing that both finally lie in the dust.
challenge.q: How does the example of the two people strengthen Job’s argument?

answers: Death removes the outward difference between their earthly conditions
Bitterness is always better than peace
challenge.explanation: The two different earthly conditions ultimately lead to the same burial.
challenge.q: What message is implied by placing abundance and bitterness side by side?

answers: It emphasizes the abundance and comfort he enjoyed
It proves that he was sick
challenge.explanation: Full breasts and moistened bones portray health, abundance, and ease.
challenge.q: Why is the description of the well-fed person important?

paragraphs.title: The Failure of the Friends’ Consolations

answers: It has been destroyed or disappeared
easy.explanation: Job quotes their question, “Where is the house of the prince?”
easy.q: What do Job’s friends say about the house of the prince?

answers: Those who go by the way
easy.explanation: Job asks whether they have questioned those who go by the way.
easy.q: Whom does Job tell them to ask?

easy.explanation: Job says their answers comfort him in vain because falsehood remains in them.
easy.q: How does Job describe the comfort given by his friends?

answers: That the ruin of a house necessarily proves wickedness
That the wicked sometimes live in peace
medium.explanation: Job rejects the assumption that the condition of a house proves the owner’s wickedness.
medium.q: What claim of his friends does Job reject?

answers: They contain error and do not truly comfort him
medium.explanation: Their arguments are false or inadequate, so they leave Job without genuine comfort.
medium.q: What does “falsehood” in Job’s final statement indicate about the friends’ answers?

answers: The wicked are reserved for the day of destruction
There are no houses in the world
medium.explanation: Travelers can observe that the wicked may be reserved for the day of destruction.
medium.q: What do travelers know about the wicked?

answers: He notes that the wicked may be brought honorably to the grave
He says every person dies alone
He says every house is destroyed immediately
challenge.explanation: Job says the wicked may be brought to the grave and remain in the tomb.
challenge.q: How does Job challenge the idea that the wicked are always recognizable by their fate?

answers: They ignore Job’s evidence and indirectly accuse him
They speak about music instead of death
challenge.explanation: They continue to rely on a simple theory of punishment despite Job’s contrary observations.
challenge.q: Why do the friends’ consolations fail?

answers: Both prove that the wicked vanish immediately
Both challenge the claim that outward fate always reveals simple divine retribution
challenge.explanation: Job argues that neither a ruined house nor a person’s burial automatically proves the friends’ theory.
challenge.q: How are the question about the house and the words about burial related?

short_answers.question: What common fate do the two contrasting people share?
short_answers.answer: They both lie down alike in the dust, and the worms cover them.
short_answers.explanation: Job emphasizes that people with very different lives share the same burial.

short_answers.question: What does Job say remains in his friends’ answers?
short_answers.explanation: He asks how they comfort him in vain when falsehood remains in their answers.
